newsitem.title: LEBANON: Banks say deficit endangers Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: Banks say deficit endangers Lebanon.

text.p: The head of the powerful Lebanese Banks Association added his voice on Wednesday to demands for the government of billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri to curb its ballooning budget deficit and lower interest rates.

In an outspoken speech, association chairman Francois Bassil said the deficit and mounting public debt were endangering all that Hariri had achieved since he took office four years ago and launched a drive to rebuild Lebanon from 16 years of civil war.

"The rapid growth of the budget deficit and the public debt connected with it threatens everything that has been achieved since 1993 with serious dangers," Bassil told the association's annual luncheon in honour of central bank Governor Riad Salameh.

Bassil's warnings follow a report last week that Lebanon's economic growth fell in the first quarter below three percent -- its lowest since Hariri took office in October 1993 and well below the 10 percent target in his national reconstruction plan.
The slowdown is widely blamed on the high interest rates on government treasury bills which finance government deficit spending and suck in most of the available funds in Lebanon.
Since Hariri took office in October 1993 the government has failed repeatedly to meet targets set in the annual budget law.
This year's target of a 36 percent deficit of income against expenditure is being massively exceeded as the deficit reached 60.2 percent in May.

Bassil said the government's methods of financing reconstruction were preventing interest rates from falling and depriving the private sector of capital by driving savings and capital inflows into liquid placements.
The government had to re-think totally its reconstruction programme and funding in order to match its effort to the resources available to Lebanon, he said.
"We believe that a deep and fast reconsideration of all planned scenarios must be carried out with the aim of balancing expenditure with abilities," Bassil said.
"It is not possible to continue rebuilding services and infrastructure through borrowing by means of treasury bills, since the servicing of the debt has come to equal public revenues," he added.
He urged the government to get the private sector more involved in reconstruction and to cap the public debt at current levels and gradually restructure it on a low-cost, long-term basis.
"Among the solutions we see is to follow a plan to cap the public debt and transfer it gradually from short-term, high cost debt to long-term, low cost," he said.

Lebanon's debt has more than tripled since December 1993 from nearly 5,000 billion Lebanese pounds to 17,504 billion ($11.4 billion) at the end of March. This is nearly 83 percent of the estimated GDP of $13.9 billion at end 1996.

Interest rates on treasury bills issued to finance the debt reached 40 percent in 1995. They are now at 13-16 percent but bankers say they need to fall another two points if the economy is to emerge from the slowdown.
Banque Audi, a leading Beirut bank, said last week first quarter economic growth was less than three percent on an annual basis and called for interest rates to come down to 14 percent.
Central bank Governor Salameh has said twice in the past two weeks that interest rates cannot drop further until the government curbs the budget deficit.
He repeated in a speech at Wednesday's lunch that rates would only fall within narrow margins in the next few months.
